questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: Why do very large chunks reduce vector retrieval precision?
options: The embedding model refuses inputs above its limit and skips the chunk entirely
The single embedding blends multiple topics, pulling the vector away from any focused query
The vector database compresses long vectors more aggressively, losing numeric precision
The reranker cannot score long passages, so large chunks get dropped from the candidates

questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: With 500-token chunks and 100-token overlap, what stride does the sliding window advance by, and what happens to index size versus no overlap?
options: Stride of 500, with index size unchanged because overlap reuses the existing vectors
Stride of 100, with index size growing fivefold because each token repeats five times
Stride of 600, with index size shrinking because chunks extend past the old boundaries
Stride of 400, with index size growing about 25% because more chunks cover the document

questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: A compliance answer keeps failing because the deciding sentence sits exactly where one 500-token chunk ends and the next begins. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Add overlap so consecutive chunks repeat boundary tokens and the sentence survives whole
Raise top-k so both halves of the sentence are retrieved and the model reassembles them
Switch to a larger embedding model so the truncated halves embed with higher fidelity
Lower the BM25 k1 parameter so term frequency saturates and boundary terms score higher

questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: A support knowledge base answers short factoid questions, but the relevant 1,500-token chunks rank below off-topic ones in vector search. What is the most likely cause?
options: The queries are too short for BM25 to compute stable inverse document frequencies
The vector index needs more partitions before long vectors can be searched accurately
The chunk embeddings blend several topics each, so no focused query lands near them
The reranker was trained on short passages and penalizes chunks above 1,000 tokens

questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: After raising chunk overlap to 50%, users report that answers cite the same passage twice and miss supporting facts. Which mechanism explains the regression?
options: Overlap doubles token counts per chunk, so the context window truncates the final chunks
Overlap causes BM25 document frequencies to drop, deflating scores for repeated terms
Adjacent chunks sharing half their text earn near-identical scores and crowd out other hits
Overlapping chunks share embedding vectors, so the ANN index collapses them into one entry

questions.topic: Chunk Size and Overlap: The Core Tradeoffs
questions.question: A 900-token chunk indexes without errors, yet queries matching only its final paragraph never retrieve it, while BM25 finds it fine. What most likely happened?
options: The ANN index quantized the vector and the error concentrated in the final paragraph
The embedding model silently truncated input past its token cap, so the tail never shaped the vector
The overlap window consumed the final paragraph, assigning its tokens to the next chunk
The chunk exceeded the reranker's window, so its score came from the opening text only

questions.question: In recursive splitting with a separator hierarchy, what happens when a paragraph still exceeds the chunk size limit?
options: The paragraph is dropped from the index and logged for manual chunking afterwards
The paragraph is embedded as one oversized chunk flagged for downstream truncation
The splitter merges it with the next paragraph so boundaries align with the size limit
The splitter retries with progressively weaker separators such as sentences, then words

questions.question: What signal does semantic chunking use to decide where one chunk ends and the next begins?
options: A spike in cosine distance between embeddings of adjacent sentences or sentence windows
A drop in BM25 term overlap between candidate chunk halves across a sliding boundary
A change in named entities detected by a tagger run across consecutive paragraphs
A shift in sentence length distribution measured against the document's own average

questions.question: Financial reports are chunked at a fixed 400 tokens, and queries about quarterly figures retrieve fragments of tables that read as gibberish. What is the right fix?
options: Enable overlap so each table row repeats across two chunks and can be reassembled
Use a structure-aware splitter that treats tables as atomic units, even when oversized
Apply semantic chunking so embedding distances place boundaries between table rows
Shrink chunks to 100 tokens so each row becomes its own precisely matched chunk

questions.question: You must chunk thousands of meeting transcripts with no headings, no paragraphs, and rambling topic shifts. Which approach fits best?
options: Markdown header splitting, because transcripts gain implicit structure from speaker turns
Fixed-size splitting with heavy overlap, because topic boundaries cannot be estimated
Semantic chunking, because embedding distance spikes can find unmarked topic shifts
Code-style syntax splitting, because utterances behave like statements inside a block

questions.question: A team proposes semantic chunking for a well-structured Markdown knowledge base. Which consideration most argues against it?
options: Header-based splitting is deterministic and usually matches or beats it there, at far lower cost
Semantic chunking cannot run on Markdown because embeddings fail on markup tokens
Percentile thresholds cannot be computed on documents with fewer than 100 sentences
Semantic chunks are always larger than header sections, so precision necessarily drops

questions.question: An engineer lowers a semantic chunker's breakpoint threshold from the 95th to the 80th percentile of adjacent-sentence distances. What should they expect?
options: Fewer, larger chunks, because more sentence pairs now fall below the boundary threshold
Identical chunking, because percentile thresholds rescale with the distance distribution
Fewer boundaries overall, because the 80th percentile is a stricter cut than the 95th
More, smaller chunks, because milder topic shifts now clear the boundary threshold

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: Why does the isolated chunk `Returns are accepted within 30 days` perform poorly in a multi-product index?
options: Its embedding is too short to reach the dimensionality that the vector index expects
Its BM25 term weights are dominated by stopwords, so it ranks for irrelevant queries
It lost the document context naming its product, so it matches return queries for all products
It contains numerals, and standard text analyzers strip numeric tokens before indexing

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: In LLM-based contextual enrichment (contextual retrieval), what exactly gets indexed?
options: The chunk with a short LLM-written context prepended, feeding both the embedding and BM25
The chunk alone, with the LLM context stored as metadata used only for display and citation
The full document summary, replacing the raw chunk text in both indexes for precision
The chunk's embedding averaged with the whole document's embedding to restore context

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: Queries like `Acme termination notice period` miss the relevant clause chunk, which reads only `The notice period is 60 days`. Which cheap index-time fix helps most?
options: Increase chunk overlap so neighboring clauses carry the notice period text as well
Raise top-k on the vector side so weakly matching clause chunks still reach assembly
Re-embed the corpus with a larger model that captures legal phrasing more precisely
Prepend a breadcrumb with the contract title and heading path to each chunk at indexing

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: LLM enrichment of a 2,000-chunk corpus looks unaffordable because every call includes the full source document. What makes it affordable in practice?
options: Batching all chunks of a document into one call so the model enriches them jointly
Prompt caching, since the document is a stable prefix reused across all its chunks' calls
Truncating each document to its first page before enrichment to shrink every prompt
Switching enrichment to the embedding model, which prices inputs far below LLM rates

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: Months after adding LLM-written chunk contexts, retrieval confidently surfaces chunks that do not answer the matched queries, and audits show the prefixes assert facts absent from the sources. What went wrong?
options: The breadcrumbs duplicated header text, so BM25 overweighted heading terms at query time
The enrichment model hallucinated, planting confident falsehoods that attract mismatched queries
The embeddings drifted because the vector database re-quantized old vectors during compaction
The prompt cache served stale document prefixes, so contexts described the wrong revision

questions.topic: Contextual Chunk Enrichment: Titles, Headers, Summaries
questions.question: A heavily edited wiki uses LLM contextual enrichment. Which operational risk deserves the most attention?
options: Chunk contexts silently going stale after edits unless re-enrichment is wired into re-indexing
Embedding vectors expiring inside the vector store and needing scheduled refresh writes
Prompt caches growing without bound until the enrichment pipeline exhausts its memory
BM25 postings fragmenting over time until lexical recall degrades below vector recall
